title: Sebastian and the Bell
premise: Coral Villalobos hosts a small-town overnight radio show, and for seven years the dead have been calling in—voices she's convinced are pranks, grief, or her own unraveling mind. When she begins recording herself sleeping to prove she's sane, the tapes capture a second voice answering questions Coral never asked aloud: a girl named Odile, taken in 1974, who wants something returned. As the calls grow more insistent and the people around Coral start remembering things they shouldn't, she uncovers that her own family profited from what was buried beneath the old Bell farm well. To survive, Coral must descend into the refilling well and give back what was stolen—but returning it means surrendering the identity she built to hide behind. In the end, Coral gives back not just the object but her name, letting Odile finally rest while Coral emerges as someone new, alive because she stopped pretending she was never there.
about_author: Wren Montrose is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who spent a decade in empty studios and swears every station has one room nobody uses. They write horror about quiet people whose silence stops working.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. During her 2 a.m. show, a caller describes his own funeral from last Tuesday in perfect detail; Coral logs it as a prank and moves on. The beat is controlled denial—we see how practiced her explanations have become, and how lonely the ritual of them is.

chapters.title: The Sleep Tapes
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Her therapist suggests recording her nights to rule out parasomnia. Reviewing the first tape, she hears herself answer questions she doesn't remember being asked—and a second voice, dry as paper, saying 'thank you.' The emotional beat: the first hairline crack in seven years of rationalization.

chapters.title: Odile
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Over three nights, the second voice names itself: Odile Bell, eleven years old, missing since June 1974. She asks Coral polite, terrible questions—'Do you still have it?' Coral researches the Bells at the library and finds the family erased from county records. Beat: dread sharpening into obsession.

chapters.title: The Well on Route 9
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She drives to the collapsed Bell farm and finds the well capped with a concrete slab stamped with her grandfather's masonry mark. A passing neighbor warns her off with a fear too old for gossip. Beat: the past is physically close, and her family's hands are on it.

chapters.title: Callers Who Aren't Callers
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, intercut with listener emails. More dead listeners call in, and now they all ask about 'the girl under the water.' Her station manager notices the show's ratings spiking among people who swear they've never tuned in. Beat: isolation deepens—the phenomenon is spreading beyond her headphones.

chapters.title: What Grandfather Took
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. In her mother's attic she finds a 1974 newspaper clipping, a child's shoebox, and a ledger showing payments to her grandfather labeled 'well work.' Inside the box: a tarnished hand bell wrapped in a christening gown. Beat: loyalty to family memory collides with the truth of what it was built on.

chapters.title: Mother Knows the Tune
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Coral and her mother, Ruthie. When Coral hums a melody from her dreams, Ruthie goes white and hums the rest—she's known the song since childhood and was told never to sing it aloud. Beat: betrayal and tenderness; Ruthie isn't a villain, just another survivor of the price.

chapters.title: The Second Voice Answers Back
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. On tape, Odile answers questions Coral asked only in her head, including one about her real name—one Coral hasn't used since she left her hometown at nineteen. Beat: horror turns intimate; the thing in the well knows who she actually is.

chapters.title: Ratings from the Grave
chapters.summary: Station manager Dev's POV. Dev investigates the impossible call log—every 'prank' caller died within the week—and finds Coral's employment file lists a start date seven years before the station opened. Beat: the world's paperwork is rotting around Coral; invisibility is failing structurally.

chapters.title: The Refill
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. At the well, the slab is wet though it hasn't rained. Water seeps upward. Odile's voice, audible without any recorder now, explains: the well refills every fifty years, and what was thrown down must be given back before it takes on its own. Beat: a deadline is set—autumn equinox, six weeks out.

chapters.title: Everyone Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Multiple short POVs—Ruthie, Dev, an elderly parishioner. Each privately remembers fragments of 1974: a procession, a bell, a vote taken in the church basement. Each decides, independently, to say nothing. Beat: communal complicity; the town's survival was purchased once and everyone held the receipt.

chapters.title: The Question Tape
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She spends a night asking the recording direct questions and gets a full accounting: in 1974 the town drowned the Bell family's 'cursed' bell in the well with Odile inside it, and paid her grandfather to seal it. The price of their survival transfers to whoever holds the secret. Beat: fury and nausea; Coral has been paying interest on a debt she never signed.

chapters.title: Dev Digs
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Following the impossible employment record, Dev finds Coral's original application—signed with a name that isn't Coral Villalobos. He confronts her gently; she denies nothing and asks him to forget it. He can't. Beat: identity theme surfaces; even her alias is fraying.

chapters.title: Ruthie's Confession
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Ruthie admits she was nine in 1974, saw the procession, and was made to carry the christening gown home afterward. She kept the box, then gave it to Coral unknowingly through the attic. Beat: generational guilt passed like an heirloom; mother and daughter grieve together for the first time.

chapters.title: The Calls Stop Being Polite
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Dead callers now speak in unison, reciting Coral's birth name on air until she cuts the mic. Listeners report hearing it too. Her carefully constructed life—apartment, job, invented surname—begins literally unwriting itself; her lease can't be found. Beat: panic; the cost of hiding comes due all at once.

chapters.title: Equinox Eve
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. With one night left, Coral packs the bell, the gown, and the ledger. Ruthie begs her to run instead; Dev offers to come. Coral realizes running only moves the debt to someone else—probably Dev, probably a child. Beat: the choice crystallizes; survival at others' expense is the thing she refuses.

chapters.title: Down the Well
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She pries the slab and descends on a rope into rising black water, ringing the bell as she goes so Odile can find her. The walls remember everything—every voice the town ever drowned. Beat: claustrophobic climax approach; courage as a form of honesty.

chapters.title: The Girl Under the Water
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, submerged and dreamlike. Odile appears as both drowned child and grown woman—the years the well stole. Coral returns the bell, the gown, the ledger, and offers the only thing left: her hidden name, spoken aloud in the dark. Beat: climax; truth as literal currency, freely paid.

chapters.title: What the Water Takes
chapters.summary: Dual POV, Coral and Odile. Odile accepts—not Coral's life, but the name, the weight of being unseen. The water pulls Odile free of the well's hunger; Coral nearly drowns holding onto the rope Dev threw. Beat: sacrifice without death; the price is selfhood, not blood.

chapters.title: Morning, Unlisted Number
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. He hauls Coral out at dawn. The well is dry, the slab cracked clean through. Coral remembers her childhood name but says it feels like a coat she's outgrown. The dead callers' numbers are disconnected—for good. Beat: exhausted relief; survival redefined as change rather than concealment.

chapters.title: The Last Broadcast
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. On air, Coral tells the whole story—1974, the ledger, her grandfather, her real name—to a listening town. Some hang up. Some don't. Ruthie calls in and sings the melody, complete, in daylight. Beat: catharsis; loyalty to truth over loyalty to silence.

chapters.title: Static, Then Nothing
chapters.summary: Epilogue, mixed POVs across a year. The show ends; Coral trains Dev to take over and leaves town with no forwarding address—by choice this time. In a thrift store two states away, a hand bell rings once on its shelf, gently, like a wave goodbye. Final beat: peace with a faint chill; some debts end, some just go quiet.
